props.title: Sorrowful Jones
props.initialSlug: When love's the stakes, the odds are high.

sections.content: Bob Hope delivers one of his most nuanced dramatic-comedy performances in **Sorrowful Jones** (1949), a heartwarming remake of Little Miss Marker (1934) which had originally starred Shirley Temple. The film represents a fascinating intersection of post-war American cinema's attempt to blend comedy with more serious themes. Like The Kid (1921) and Little Miss Marker (1934) before it, Sorrowful Jones explores the transformative power of an unexpected parent-child relationship, with Hope playing a hardened bookie whose life changes when he's forced to care for a young girl left as collateral for a bet.

sections.content: The Damon Runyon source material, which spawned multiple adaptations including **40 Pounds of Trouble** (1962) and **Little Miss Marker** (1980), proves particularly effective in its 1949 incarnation. Hope, known primarily for his rapid-fire one-liners and fourth-wall-breaking comedy in films like **Road to Morocco** (1942), shows remarkable restraint and genuine pathos. His chemistry with young Mary Jane Saunders creates moments of authentic tenderness rarely seen in his other work.

The film's Broadway-tinged underworld, populated by colorful gangsters and gamblers, became a template for later films like Guys and Dolls (1955) and Pocketful of Miracles (1961). Director Sidney Lanfield, who previously worked with Hope on **The Big Broadcast of 1938** (1938), effectively balances the story's lighter moments with its more dramatic elements, creating a film that stands as one of the more successful comedy-drama hybrids of the late 1940s. sections.content: **Sorrowful Jones** (1949) marks a significant departure from Hope's established screen persona, anticipating his later dramatic work in films like **The Seven Little Foys** (1955). The film demonstrates Hollywood's growing sophistication in mixing genres, predating similar comedy-drama combinations like **The Apartment** (1960) and **Father Goose** (1964). Hope's performance influenced later comedic actors attempting dramatic roles, from Jerry Lewis in **The King of Comedy** (1982) to Adam Sandler in **Punch-Drunk Love** (2002).
